title: The Feverish Friend
twist: A hot person shivering seems backwards. His body isn't too cold at all — his brain's thermostat has been turned up, so a normal temperature suddenly feels cold.
briefing: Tomás, 13, starts sneezing at a sleepover. By 10 p.m. he's under two blankets with his teeth chattering, saying he's freezing — but when his friend's mom feels his forehead, it's hot. Around 2 a.m. he kicks the blankets off, sweating.
question: How can someone be hot and shivering at the same time?

clues.title: Hot forehead
clues.text: The thermometer reads 101 °F. His normal is about 98.6 °F.
clues.shows: his body already above its normal temperature

clues.title: Freezing under blankets
clues.text: He's shivering hard and says he feels cold, even under two blankets in a warm room.
clues.shows: his body acting as if it were too cold

clues.title: A cold since the afternoon
clues.text: He's had a runny nose and scratchy throat since lunch. His friends think he caught a cold at school.
clues.shows: his immune system busy fighting germs

clues.title: Sweating at 2 a.m.
clues.text: In the night the shivering stops. He throws off the blankets and sweats as his temperature drifts back toward normal.
clues.shows: the body switching from heating up to cooling down

hypotheses.text: The room is cold, so he's shivering.
hypotheses.flaw: His forehead is hot at 101 °F and everyone else in the room is comfortable — a cold room would make his skin cool, not hot.

hypotheses.text: Being sick makes the body lose control of its temperature at random.
hypotheses.flaw: The pattern isn't random: first he shivers to heat up, later he sweats to cool down. That's a controlled system aiming for a target.

hypotheses.text: His immune system is fighting germs and has turned up the brain's thermostat, so at his normal temperature he feels too cold and shivers to heat up; when the fight eases, the thermostat drops and he sweats to cool off.
The blankets are making him overheat.
hypotheses.flaw: Overheating makes you sweat and want to cool down — not shiver and pull blankets closer.

prediction.prompt: An hour after the fight starts, how does Tomás's body temperature depend on how hard his immune system is fighting — from no germs up to a big fight?

second.question: Right at the start of the fight, before his temperature catches up, does he feel hot or cold?

concepts.label: the immune system
concepts.hint: Which body system responds to germs?

concepts.label: the thermostat is turned up
concepts.hint: What in the brain decides what temperature counts as 'normal'?

concepts.label: shivering to heat up
concepts.hint: Why shiver if you're already hot?

concepts.label: sweating to cool down
concepts.hint: What happened at 2 a.m., and why?

transfer.context: Nia, 14, has a cold. On a warm afternoon she suddenly gets goosebumps, wants a sweater, and her temperature reads 100.5 °F.
options: The air conditioning in her house is too strong.
Her immune system turned up her brain's thermostat, so her normal temperature now feels too cold and she tries to warm up.
Colds always make people feel hot, so she must be imagining it.
She's cold because she skipped lunch.
transfer.retryHint: Hot by the thermometer but feeling cold — which of Tomás's clues was exactly that?
transfer.explanation: Nia's body is doing what Tomás's did. While her immune system fights the cold, her brain's target temperature goes up. Until her body reaches it, she feels cold — goosebumps and wanting a sweater are her body trying to heat up to the new target.

takeaway: A fever isn't the body losing control — it's the immune system turning the brain's thermostat up while it fights germs. Shivering heats you to the new target; sweating cools you down when the target drops again.
